body: The legendary frameworks differ in emphasis but share a core: an understandable business with high, durable returns on capital, honest owner-minded management, low debt, a price below conservative value, and a long hold. Buffett's four filters are a business "(1) that we can understand; (2) with favorable long-term prospects; (3) operated by honest and competent people; and (4) available at a very attractive price" ([1977 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1977.html)). He also argued it is "far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price" ([1989 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1989.html)). Munger's quote is the bridge between cheapness and quality. A business earning 6% on capital for 40 years returns about 6% even if bought at a big discount, while one earning 18% gives "one hell of a result" even at an expensive-looking price ([Farnam Street transcript](https://fs.blog/great-talks/a-lesson-on-worldly-wisdom/)). Terry Smith compresses it into "buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing," with holdings typically earning **25–30% ROCE** ([Fundsmith](https://www.fundsmith.co.uk/news/2015/2171-this-is-money-firms-which-provide-good-products-or-services-are-key-to-investing-says-fundsmith-boss/); [Trustnet](https://www.trustnet.com/news/662915/three-simple-steps-to-making-returns-like-terry-smith)). Lynch adds categories (slow growers, stalwarts, fast growers, cyclicals, turnarounds, asset plays) and the PEG ratio, where a fairly priced P/E equals the growth rate ([Value Research](https://www.valueresearchonline.com/stories/51021/peter-lynch-s-six-stock-categories/)). Nick Sleep's "scale economics shared" explains Costco and Amazon. The firm passes savings from scale to customers, which drives volume and still lower costs ([Morningstar AU](https://www.morningstar.com.au/insights/personal-finance/254055/my-favourite-lessons-from-nick-sleeps-famous-investing-letters)). Mayer's 100-bagger traits are high sustained ROE, owner-operators, small starting size, a moat, a reasonable starting multiple and a "coffee can" hold ([Mindful Compounding](https://mindfulcompounding.substack.com/p/what-i-learned-from-chris-mayer); [Hedge Fund Alpha](https://hedgefundalpha.com/strategies/christopher-mayers-notes-100-baggers/)).

title: AI stock picking playbook › Legends, Indian masters and quant firms converge on quality bought at a sensible price

body:
- A combined Indian checklist would include:
  - 10 years of revenue growth ≥10% and ROCE ≥15% every year (Marcellus).
  - CFO/EBITDA ≥ about 70–80% over 5–10 years, with clean forensic flags.
  - Promoter integrity: low pledge, sensible related-party transactions, a credible auditor.
  - A small size with a large runway (SQGLP/SMILE).
  - An entry P/E that leaves room for rerating (QGLP "P").
  - A long holding period.
- Motilal's evidence across its studies and Mayer's US 100-bagger work point to the same mechanism. The biggest winners came from earnings compounding *plus* multiple expansion. Paying a very high starting P/E removes the second engine.
- The 30th study's sector mix (financials, industrials, capital markets) reflects the 2020–25 cycle. It should not be read as a permanent rule.
